passage:
At the district hospital's children's ward, Aditi had one strong first impression of the new nurse, Ishita: late for her first shift, hair still wet, charts left half-filled. In her small notebook Aditi wrote: "Ishita, seems careless. (Guess. Day one.)" Underneath: "What would change my mind? On time for a week. Charts complete. Good with the kids."
Over the next ten days Aditi watched without comment. Ishita came early every day after that first one; her bus route had changed, it turned out. Her charts were tidy. On night shift she sat for an hour with a frightened boy until he slept.
Aditi crossed out "careless" and wrote "rough first day". At tea she said, "I misjudged you at first. Sorry. Want to swap tips on the new chart system?"

qa.q: What did Aditi write in her notebook on day one?
qa.a: "Ishita, seems careless. (Guess. Day one.)"

qa.q: Why did Aditi add 'Guess. Day one.' to her note?
qa.a: She felt cautious about her first impression, knowing it can be wrong, and wanted to remind herself that one late, rushed shift was very little evidence.

qa.q: What made Aditi's approach fair?
qa.a: She wrote down in advance what would change her mind, watched for it quietly, and updated her view when the evidence came.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel when Aditi apologises at tea?
qa.a: Ishita might feel relieved and welcomed, and more at ease in the new ward. 🙂

grounding: It shows a woman treating her first impression as a guess and looking for evidence that could change her mind.

passage:
Dear Leela didi,
The new flatmate, Rafiq, moved in on Saturday. My first impression, honestly? Loud. He played music till eleven and left a pan in the sink overnight. I caught myself deciding "this will be a nightmare" within an hour.
So I'm trying what you taught me. I've written that impression down as a guess, not a fact. Then I made a list of what would change my mind: does he fix things when asked, does he pay his share on time, how does he treat the cleaning aunty.
It's day five. He turned the music down the moment I asked. He paid the electricity bill early. He talks to Kamla aunty like she's family. The pan is still a problem.
I'm keeping the notebook going. I suspect I'll be wrong in a good way.
Your little sister,
Vinita

qa.q: What did Rafiq do when Vinita asked about the music?
qa.a: He turned the music down the moment she asked.

qa.q: Why did Vinita write her first impression down as a guess?
qa.a: She noticed she'd decided 'this will be a nightmare' within an hour and wanted to stop that quick judgement from hardening into a fact.

qa.q: Why is Vinita's list of what would change her mind useful?
qa.a: It tells her exactly what evidence to watch for, so she can update fairly instead of noticing only things that fit her first view.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel if Vinita had treated her first impression as fact?
qa.a: He might feel judged and unwelcome from day one, even though he turned the music down and paid the bill early.

grounding: It shows a woman holding her first impression of a flatmate lightly and deliberately looking for evidence that could change it.

passage: People ask how I hire. I'm Ankita, I run a small design studio in Kochi, and my amma likes to call me her slow-to-judge daughter. It wasn't always true. Two years ago a candidate called Francis walked in, barely looked up, and mumbled his answers. In the first minute I thought, "Not confident, won't manage clients." Then I remembered I'd been exactly that nervous at my first interview. So I told myself: that's a guess. What would prove it wrong? I asked him to redo one of our old client briefs overnight. The next morning he sent three ideas, clear and clever, with notes a client could understand. On his third day he presented to a client himself. Now I write my first impression on a sticky note and try to disprove it.

qa.q: What task did Ankita give Francis overnight?
qa.a: To redo one of the studio's old client briefs.

qa.q: What made Ankita stop and treat her first thought as a guess?
qa.a: She remembered being just as nervous at her own first interview, so she doubted that mumbling meant he couldn't manage clients.

qa.q: How does the sticky-note habit help Ankita hire fairly?
qa.a: Writing the first impression down and then trying to disprove it makes her look for evidence instead of trusting the first minute.

qa.q: What would have happened to Francis if Ankita had trusted her first impression?
qa.a: He might never have been hired, and the studio would have missed someone who presented to a client on his third day.

grounding: It shows a woman treating a first impression as a guess and testing it with evidence that could change her mind.

passage:
I'm Rehana, and I've taught next door to Zainab for a year at the primary school in Lucknow. I saw how she handled Mr Qureshi.
At the first parent-teacher meeting he stormed in, raised his voice about his son's marks, and walked out before she could answer. The rest of us decided he was a bully. Zainab wrote in her diary, and I saw the line: "First impression: angry, rude. But this is a guess."
Then she did something I didn't. She asked the office when he usually picked up his son. She waited at the gate one evening. She found out he worked nights at the railway yard and had rushed in straight from a shift.
The next month she called him at a time that suited him. He apologised before she said anything.
I still don't know exactly what she was thinking. But she never treated that first meeting as the whole man.

qa.q: Where did Mr Qureshi work?
qa.a: He worked nights at the railway yard.

qa.q: How did Zainab seem to feel about her first impression of Mr Qureshi, and what shows it?
qa.a: Zainab seemed cautious and doubtful about her first impression, writing "But this is a guess" and then finding out he had rushed in straight from a night shift.

qa.q: Which steps by Zainab changed the outcome?
qa.a: Finding out when he picked up his son, talking to him at the gate, and calling at a time that suited him, which gave her new evidence and led to his apology.

qa.q: How might Mr Qureshi have felt when Zainab called at a time that suited him?
qa.a: He may have felt respected and a little embarrassed about the first meeting, which is perhaps why he apologised before she said anything.

grounding: It shows a wise person holding a first impression lightly, noting it is a guess, and looking for evidence that could change her mind.

passage:
Monday: On Shalini's first day at the Shillong newsroom, the new intern corrected Lalremsiami's headline in front of the editor. "It should be 'fewer', not 'less'." Lalremsiami, twenty-five, felt her face burn. That evening she wrote in her notes: "First impression: show-off. Only a guess. What would prove me wrong?"
Wednesday: She asked to see Shalini's first three drafts. They were careful and clear. At lunch she noticed Shalini quietly helping the photographer caption forty pictures before a deadline, asking nothing in return.
Friday: Shalini came to her desk. "I'm sorry about Monday. I was nervous and I blurted it. I should have told you privately."
Lalremsiami crossed out "show-off" in her notes and wrote "careful, nervous, kind". "It was right, though," she said. "Fewer. Want to check my next one?"

qa.q: What did Shalini correct in Lalremsiami's headline?
qa.a: Shalini said it should be 'fewer', not 'less'.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling on Monday, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, her face burning, but she wrote her impression down as only a guess and asked herself what would prove her wrong.

qa.q: Which choice helped Lalremsiami change her mind fairly?
qa.a: Looking at Shalini's drafts and watching how Shalini treated others gave real evidence beyond the first awkward moment.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel when Lalremsiami asks for a check of the next headline?
qa.a: Shalini is likely relieved and pleased, feeling forgiven and trusted after a nervous first day.

grounding: It shows a wise person holding a first impression lightly, noting it as a guess, and deliberately looking for evidence that would change her mind.

passage: Jahnavi, you've already decided the new hire is lazy, after one morning? Let me, your old senior Sudha, tell you what I learned at twenty-five. In my first year running a small team at the bank, a young man named Rakesh joined. On his first day he barely greeted anyone and left at exactly five. My first thought was: proud, not a team player. But I had a habit from my mother: when you judge someone quickly, write it down with 'guess' beside it. So I wrote: 'Rakesh, proud? Guess.' Then I watched for anything that would prove me wrong. By the second week I had it: he left at five to collect his little sister from school, and his reports were the cleanest on the floor. He was just shy. Without that word 'guess', I'd have treated him as proud for years.

qa.q: Why did Rakesh leave at exactly five?
qa.a: He left at five to collect his little sister from school.

qa.q: Why did young Sudha write 'guess' beside the first impression?
qa.a: Sudha felt tempted to judge quickly but stayed cautious, knowing a first thought about someone is only a guess until tested.

qa.q: What was the key choice in Sudha's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Writing 'guess' and then watching for evidence that would prove it wrong, which revealed the little sister and the clean reports.

qa.q: What might Rakesh's first weeks have been like?
qa.a: Rakesh was shy and juggling his sister's school pickup, probably unaware that anyone had thought him proud.

grounding: Shows a young manager holding a first impression lightly, labelling it a guess, and looking for evidence that would change it.

passage: Bhavna's first morning as supervisor at the food-testing lab in Indore did not start well. Wasim, the senior technician, came in forty minutes late, muttered a greeting and put on his headphones. Careless, she thought, and then, as she had trained herself to, added: first impression, not a fact. Let's see. At noon the power went out across the industrial area, with sixty milk samples due at the dairy by evening. The backup generator coughed and died. Bhavna was about to call head office when Wasim pulled off his headphones, found a spare fuel line in a drawer, and had the generator running in ten minutes. Then he relabelled every sample by torchlight. At six, the samples went out on time. Later she learned he had come in late after a night at the hospital with his mother. She crossed 'careless' out of her notebook.

qa.q: How many milk samples were due at the dairy by evening?
qa.a: Sixty milk samples were due by evening.

qa.q: What was Bhavna thinking when Wasim came in late and put on headphones?
qa.a: Bhavna felt irritated and thought he was careless, but deliberately reminded herself it was only a first impression to test.

qa.q: Why was Bhavna's habit of noting 'first impression, not a fact' useful here?
qa.a: It kept her open, so Wasim's quick fix and the reason for his lateness could change her view instead of being ignored.

qa.q: What might Wasim's day have been like?
qa.a: Wasim came in exhausted after a night at the hospital with his mother, yet still saved the samples.

grounding: Shows a young supervisor treating a bad first impression as a guess and letting later evidence change her mind.

passage: When Sunaina moved into the two-bedroom flat in Baner, her new flatmate Nikita said hello without looking up from her laptop and shut her door. Cold, Sunaina thought, unpacking. Then she caught herself. She had been wrong about people before, and had promised herself to treat first impressions as rough guesses. So she made a small list on her phone: what would show I'm wrong? Nikita saying hi first. Nikita sharing something. Over the week, she watched. On Tuesday Nikita left a note: 'Water tanker comes at 7, keep buckets ready.' On Thursday there was a second balcony key on Sunaina's pillow. On Saturday Nikita knocked. "I'm terrible at first days. Want to get pav bhaji?" Sunaina laughed and grabbed her slippers.

qa.q: What did Nikita's Tuesday note say?
qa.a: The note said, 'Water tanker comes at 7, keep buckets ready.'

qa.q: Why did Sunaina write a list of what would prove the first impression wrong?
qa.a: Sunaina felt a flicker of disappointment at the cold hello but stayed curious, wanting to test the impression rather than trust it.

qa.q: Which of Sunaina's steps is worth copying, and why?
qa.a: Listing what would show she is wrong and then watching for it, because it makes her notice the note, the key and the invitation instead of only the cold hello.

qa.q: What might Nikita mean by 'I'm terrible at first days'?
qa.a: Nikita probably felt shy or awkward at first and showed care through small acts before being able to be friendly out loud.

grounding: Shows a young woman treating a cold first impression of a flatmate as a guess and looking for evidence that would change her mind.

"Kalyani, what did you think of the new project lead?"
"Honestly, Rukmini didi? Cold. She didn't smile once in the meeting."
"Hmm. I thought so too at first."
"At first?"
"I've started doing a thing. When I meet someone, I write down my first impression, but I label it: guess."
"And?"
"Then I write what would change my mind. For her: if she listens well one-on-one, or if she's kind to juniors."
"And has she?"
"Yesterday I saw her stay back with an intern for an hour, explaining the code. Very patiently."
"Oh."
"So my guess is already wobbling."
"Maybe she's just shy in big meetings."
"Maybe. I'll keep watching. It's only been two weeks."

qa.q: How long did the project lead stay back with the intern?
qa.a: For an hour, explaining the code.

qa.q: What might Rukmini be feeling when she says her guess is "already wobbling"?
qa.a: She seems curious and open, a little amused that the first impression is already being challenged.

qa.q: What is Rukmini's method, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She writes her first impression, labels it a guess, and notes what would change her mind, so she stays open to new evidence.

qa.q: How might the new project lead feel if people decided she was cold?
qa.a: She might feel misjudged and lonely, especially if she's just shy in big meetings.

grounding: Shows a mature person treating a first impression as a guess and deliberately looking for evidence that would change her mind.

passage: When Omkar joined our design team last year, I disliked him within a day. I'm Minakshi, and I'm not proud of it. He interrupted me twice in the first meeting and wore headphones all afternoon. I decided he was arrogant. But I've learned my first impressions are often wrong, so I did what I now always do. I wrote in my notebook: "First impression: arrogant. This is a guess." And then: "What would change my mind? If he credits others, if he asks for feedback, if he helps without being asked." Then I watched. In week two, he thanked a junior by name in a client meeting. In week three, he asked me to review his layout. In week five, he stayed late to fix my file. I crossed out "arrogant." We're good friends now. The headphones, it turns out, are for his tinnitus.

qa.q: What did Omkar do in week three?
qa.a: He asked Minakshi to review his layout.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling after the first meeting with Omkar?
qa.a: Minakshi felt irritated and disliked him, deciding he was arrogant after being interrupted twice.

qa.q: What did Minakshi do that others could copy?
qa.a: Minakshi labelled the first impression as a guess, wrote down what would change it, and watched for that evidence before deciding.

qa.q: How might Omkar have felt if Minakshi had kept her first impression?
qa.a: Omkar might have felt shut out and misjudged, despite crediting others and helping.

grounding: A young professional describes treating a first impression as a guess and looking for evidence that could change it.

passage:
Supervisor's note, hospital records department, 10 June.
Our new trainee, Trisha, started on Monday. My honest first impression: disinterested. She yawned in the induction and barely asked questions.
I have learned to hold first impressions lightly, so I am writing this down as a guess, not a fact.
What would change my mind: if she asks good questions one-on-one; if her work is careful; if she follows up without being chased.
Update, 24 June. Trisha has asked me five sharp questions about coding errors, all in private. Her error rate is the lowest in the batch. She mentioned she was taking the night bus from her village for the first week until she found a room.
I was wrong. Guess crossed out.
Next step: I'll put her on the audit team.
Afreen

qa.q: How many questions has Trisha asked in private by 24 June?
qa.a: Five sharp questions about coding errors.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling on first seeing Trisha yawn?
qa.a: Afreen felt doubtful and a bit disappointed, reading the yawns as disinterest.

qa.q: Which part of Afreen's approach made the difference?
qa.a: Writing the first impression as a guess and listing what would change Afreen's mind, then checking the evidence two weeks later.

qa.q: What was Trisha's first week like?
qa.a: Trisha was exhausted from taking the night bus from her village each day until she found a room.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows a young professional holding a first impression lightly and looking for evidence that could change it.

passage:
Friday, 10 p.m.
On Monday I wrote a line at the back of this diary after meeting our new colleague, Gurpreet, transferred from the Delhi office: loud laugh, interrupted our manager twice, called me "boss" within ten minutes. My verdict: show-off, will be hard to work with.
But underneath I also wrote: first guess, made in five minutes. What would change my mind? If Gurpreet listens in meetings. If Gurpreet shares credit. If the interrupting is nerves, not arrogance. Check on Friday.
So, Friday. Gurpreet stayed back two evenings to help me fix the report, and in the team call said, "Mahima found the bug." Still loud. Not a show-off.
I'm glad I wrote Monday down as a guess. Otherwise I'd have spent the week collecting proof for it.
Mahima

qa.q: Where was Gurpreet transferred from?
qa.a: Gurpreet was transferred from the Delhi office.

qa.q: Why did Mahima write the first impression down as a guess?
qa.a: Mahima felt wary of trusting a snap judgement made in five minutes, and wanted to stay open to being wrong.

qa.q: How did Mahima test the first impression?
qa.a: Mahima listed what would change the view, like listening and sharing credit, and checked it against what Gurpreet actually did by Friday.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel on hearing about Monday's note?
qa.a: Gurpreet might laugh or feel a little stung, but would probably be glad Mahima looked at the evidence.

grounding: Shows a young professional who holds a first impression lightly, notes it as a guess and looks for evidence that would change it.

passage:
On her first day as the new science teacher at the school in Bishnupur, Bidisha met the headmistress, Sonali, for exactly two minutes. Sonali didn't smile, handed her a timetable and said, "Lab key is with the peon. Don't lose it."
Walking to the classroom, Bidisha felt her face harden. Cold. Won't like me. Then she caught the thought and turned it over. Two minutes. One tired sentence. That was a guess, not a person.
So she watched. Over the next fortnight she saw Sonali stay late with a girl whose father had been hurt, walk three kilometres to a family whose son had stopped coming, and quietly pay for a boy's exam fee.
On Friday, Bidisha asked if the science club could use the lab on Saturdays. Sonali looked at her for a long moment and said, "I was hoping someone would ask."

qa.q: How long did Bidisha first meet Sonali for?
qa.a: Bidisha met the headmistress, Sonali, for exactly two minutes.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do with her first thought about Sonali?
qa.a: Bidisha felt a quick sting at the coldness, then caught the thought and treated it as a guess rather than a verdict.

qa.q: How did watching for a fortnight help Bidisha?
qa.a: It showed Sonali staying late, walking to a family and paying a fee, evidence that changed the first impression.

qa.q: How does Sonali respond when Bidisha asks about the science club?
qa.a: Sonali seems quietly pleased, saying she had hoped someone would ask.

grounding: Shows a young teacher who holds a first impression lightly and looks for evidence that would change her mind.

passage:
The first night Diego moved into the flat in Osaka, bass thumped through the thin wall until one in the morning. Yuki lay awake, jaw tight, already composing a cold message.
Instead she opened her notes and typed: "First guess: careless. Only a guess. What would change it? If he turns it down when asked. If he does his share in the kitchen."
The next evening she knocked. "The music carries a lot through this wall." Diego went red, apologised, and bought a pair of headphones that weekend.
Over the following fortnight Yuki kept adding lines: dishes washed, a note on the fridge asking about her shifts, rice left warm for her after a late one.
One night she scrolled back to that first entry, smiled, and deleted the word "careless".

qa.q: What did Diego buy after Yuki knocked?
qa.a: Diego bought a pair of headphones that weekend.

qa.q: How was Yuki feeling that first night, and what did she do with that feeling?
qa.a: She was irritated and tired, lying awake with her jaw tight, but she wrote her judgement down as only a guess and listed what would change it.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Writing "Only a guess" and naming the evidence that would change it worked, because it kept Yuki watching what Diego actually did instead of sending the cold message.

qa.q: What would it have been like for Diego if Yuki had sent the cold message?
qa.a: He might have felt judged on his first night, before he even knew the wall was thin, and the flat could have started with tension instead of warm rice.

grounding: Shows a person treating a first impression as a guess and deliberately watching for evidence that would change her mind.
